final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

comments.body:
Done — report attached, all three questions answered, nothing researched beyond them.

**Short version:** DIY the daily work, buy one $300 reactivity course for the method. HSSV's "Top Dogs Level 1" is the best pick ($300, 6 weeks, evening Zoom, built specifically for leash reactivity) — and if he was an HSSV adoption, check first whether your adopter's complimentary training covers it. Orion in San Jose (~$275–295, in-person, free 20-min consult) is the alternative if you want real-world practice. D For Dogz (650-538-3011) is the private option but won't publish prices, so you'd have to call.

**Your next moves, in order:**
1. Buy the gear — front-clip harness and a 6 ft flat leash (subtask created)
2. Start Week 1 (subtask created — the drills are written out, you don't need to look anything up)
3. Email HSSV or ring Orion if you want the course running alongside

One thing I decided for you and you should overrule me if you disagree: I ruled out e-collar and board-and-train programs entirely, including Off Leash K9 San Jose despite them having a reactivity package. For a barking-at-dogs problem those suppress the symptom and can worsen the underlying reaction.

Parent set to `needs_review` — everything left is yours to physically do.
comments.author: agent

report.markdown:
## Bottom line

**Do it yourself, but buy one structured reactivity course (~$300) for guidance.** The leash pulling is a gear-plus-consistency problem you can solve in a few weeks alone. The barking at other dogs is the part where DIY usually stalls, so pay for structure there — not for someone to take the dog away and hand him back.

Total recommended spend: **~$370–400** ($300 course + ~$70–100 gear).

---

## 1. Hire or DIY?

| | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Leash pulling** | DIY. Front-clip harness + stop-when-tight, 10 min a day. |
| **Barking/lunging at dogs** | DIY the daily reps, buy a course for the method. |
| **Full private trainer** | Hold in reserve — trigger it at the Week 4 checkpoint. |

Why not just a normal obedience class: SIRIUS, one of the biggest Bay Area schools, states that fearful or reactive dogs, or dogs barking disruptively, should do private lessons with an experienced trainer before joining a group class. HSSV likewise runs reactivity in a separate track from obedience. A generic manners class puts him in a room full of triggers and rehearses the exact behaviour you're trying to change.

**Escalate to a paid private trainer if, after four weeks:** he still can't take a treat with a dog visible at ~50 ft, he redirects onto you or the leash when triggered, or you've started avoiding walks. Expect $150–250 per in-home session locally.

**Avoid:** e-collar and "balanced" board-and-train programs. Off Leash K9 San Jose, for example, charges $500 for the first lesson bundled with an e-collar. Suppressing the bark doesn't change the emotion driving it.

---

## 2. Local options with real prices

| Option | Format | Price | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HSSV — Top Dogs Level 1** | 6 weeks, online Zoom, evening start | **$300** | ★ Best pick. Purpose-built for leash/barrier reactivity in dogs who bark, lunge or worry but haven't injured anyone. Evenings-friendly; you practice on your own walks between sessions. Contact `DogTraining@hssv.org`. **If he was adopted from HSSV, adopters get complimentary training — email them his Animal ID first.** |
| **Orion Dog Training**, San Jose | In-person group, 3,000 sq ft indoor facility | **~$275–295** for 6-week programs | Positive-reinforcement only. Dedicated reactive-dog track plus Control Unleashed and Loose Leash Walking classes. Offers a **free 20-minute phone consult** and refers out to other force-free trainers if not a fit. Good if you want real-world in-person practice. |
| **D For Dogz**, serves San Jose / Santa Clara / Sunnyvale / Campbell / Mountain View | Private in-home, day school, or group | **Not published** — advertises $420 off full enrolment, so ask for the total | Has a specific leash-reactivity protocol and a "Personal Coaching" option where they teach *you* to train the dog (ask for this one, not board & train). Hours listed Mon–Fri 9am–7pm, Sun 9am–3pm. **650-538-3011.** |

Market context so you can sanity-check any quote: private in-home sessions around Sunnyvale typically run **$150–250 per visit** with package discounts, with behaviour cases at the top of that range; group courses nationally sit at **$100–300**.

**Screening question for any trainer:** "What do you do when he barks and lunges?" If the answer involves a prong collar, e-collar, or "correcting" him, walk away.

---

## 3. The four-week plan

Gear first: front-clip/dual-clip harness (Balance Harness, PetSafe Easy Walk, or Ruffwear Front Range), 6 ft flat leash (no retractable), treat pouch, high-value soft treats, optional 15 ft long line. ~$70–100.

**Week 1 — Pressure off, foundation on.** No walks past other dogs at all; every bark is practice at barking. Daily 2×10 min: name game, driveway-only loose-leash (leash tight = you stop dead; slack = "yes" + treat), and "find it" treat scatters. One weekend 30–45 min long-line sniff walk somewhere empty. *Success: instant response to his name, and "find it" drops his nose in a second.*

**Week 2 — Find his threshold, start engage-disengage.** Threshold = the closest distance where he can still take food and look away (likely 60–100 ft). Work there. 3×/week, 10–15 min: the instant he looks at a distant dog, mark and feed. He learns to look, then check back with you. Pay him for *noticing calmly*, not for silence. If he barks, you were too close — "find it", retreat 20 ft, restart, no scolding. *Success: you know his number in feet.*

**Week 3 — Close the distance, add an escape route.** Teach a "let's go" 180° U-turn in the quiet, then use it as your rip cord on walks. Move 5–10 ft closer in engage-disengage *only* if last week was clean. Parallel-walk with a friend's calm dog at 40+ ft, same direction, no greeting. Never let him meet a dog head-on on leash — tight leash plus face-to-face is what built this. *Success: U-turn on cue, threshold shrinking.*

**Week 4 — Real walks, then decide.** Two or three normal neighbourhood walks with the full toolkit, you scanning ahead so you spot every dog before he does. Then assess: can he eat at 30–40 ft? Does a bark recover in seconds instead of escalating for a block? Is loose-leash working when no dogs are around? Mostly yes → keep repeating weeks 3–4 with shrinking distance. Mostly no → book the trainer.

**Expectation setting:** four weeks gets you a working protocol and visible progress, not a cured dog. Meaningful reactivity change runs 3–6 months. And for a 14-month collie mix, daily sniffing and mental work isn't optional enrichment — an under-drained collie is a more reactive collie.

---

## What's in the tree

Five weekly subtasks (gear + weeks 1–4) with the full drills in each description, plus one human task holding the trainer contacts and the exact questions to ask.

subtasks.title: Decide: DIY vs hire a trainer for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid — do the daily work yourself, buy one structured reactivity course/consult for guidance. ~$300 total.

Reasoning:
- Leash pulling is pure DIY territory. It's a mechanical + reinforcement problem; a front-clip harness plus consistent daily practice fixes it. No trainer needed.
- Barking/lunging at other dogs (leash reactivity) is the part where DIY commonly stalls. It needs correct distance management and reading stress signals early — that's what a course or a single consult buys you. HSSV explicitly places reactive dogs in a separate class track, and SIRIUS refuses reactive dogs in its regular group classes and tells owners to do private lessons first — a good signal that this issue needs targeted help, not a generic obedience class.
- 14 months = adolescent border collie mix; high drive, still very trainable. Timing is good.
- Constraint check: evenings/weekends only. Online reactivity class (HSSV, evening Zoom) fits this best; you practice on your own walks between sessions.

Hire a full private trainer (not just a course) if after 4 weeks of the plan: he still can't eat a treat within 50 ft of another dog, he redirects/snaps at you or the leash when triggered, or you're avoiding walks entirely. Budget $150–250 per in-home private session in the South Bay.

AVOID: e-collar / "balanced" board-and-train programs for a reactive dog (e.g. Off Leash K9 San Jose, $500 first lesson incl. e-collar). Suppressing the bark doesn't change the underlying reaction and can make it worse.

subtasks.title: Find 2-3 South Bay trainers with real prices for leash reactivity
subtasks.description:
Three options, verified prices:

1) HUMANE SOCIETY SILICON VALLEY — "Top Dogs Level 1" (BEST VALUE)
$300 for a 6-week course, entirely online via Zoom. Built specifically for dogs with leash or barrier reactivity; for dogs who bark/lunge/worry but have NOT caused injury. Evening start times (a recent cohort ran 6:15pm) so it fits evenings-only. Learn at home, then practice on real walks.
hssv.org/behavior-management-classes/ · DogTraining@hssv.org
NOTE: HSSV gives complimentary training to dogs adopted from them — if he's an HSSV adoption, email them your dog's Animal ID first.

2) ORION DOG TRAINING — San Jose, in-person
Positive-reinforcement only, 3,000 sq ft indoor climate-controlled facility, free parking. Runs a dedicated reactive-dog track plus Control Unleashed and Loose Leash Walking classes. 6-week group programs run ~$275–$295; drop-in agility $39. Offers a FREE 20-minute phone consult to check fit, and will refer out to force-free trainers in their network if they're not the right match.
oriondogtraining.com/reactivedog

3) D FOR DOGZ — private, in-home, serves San Jose/Santa Clara/Sunnyvale/Campbell/Mountain View
Uses their own leash-reactivity protocol; offers Reactive Dog Foundation as private training, day school, group class, or board & train, with a "Personal Coaching" option where they teach you to train the dog. Prices not published — they advertise ~$420 off if you enroll in the full program, so ask for the full number. Hours listed Mon–Fri 9am–7pm, Sun 9am–3pm (confirm evening slots).
Phone: 650-538-3011 · dfordogtraining.com

Market context: private in-home sessions in the Sunnyvale area typically run $150–$250 per visit with package discounts; behavior problems price at the top of that range. Group courses generally $100–$300.

Not recommended: SIRIUS ($249/5 sessions) — good school but explicitly excludes reactive dogs from group classes. Off Leash K9 San Jose — $500 first lesson bundled with an e-collar; aversive approach, wrong tool for this dog.

subtasks.title: Write the 4-week week-by-week training plan
subtasks.description: Plan written and split into five child tasks (gear + one per week). Core method: front-clip harness for the pulling, engage-disengage / counter-conditioning at sub-threshold distance for the barking, plus daily sniff-based decompression because he's a collie mix. All sessions are 10-15 min so they fit evenings; long line sniff walk on weekends. Full detail in each weekly subtask and in the report on the parent task.

subtasks.title: Buy gear before Week 1
subtasks.description: Front-clip / dual-clip harness (Balance Harness, PetSafe Easy Walk, or Ruffwear Front Range) + 6 ft flat leash (NOT retractable) + treat pouch + high-value soft treats you can deliver fast (string cheese, hot dog coins, freeze-dried liver). Optional: 15 ft long line for decompression sniff walks. No prong, no choke, no e-collar. Budget ~$70-100.

subtasks.title: Week 1 — Pressure off, foundation on
subtasks.description:
GOAL: stop rehearsing the problem while building two core skills.

Rules this week: no walks past other dogs. If a dog appears, turn and leave — every bark is practice at barking.

Daily (2x 10 min, evenings):
1. Name game / 'Look at me' — say his name, mark the head turn, feed. 20 reps indoors, then front yard.
2. Loose-leash in the driveway/cul-de-sac only. Leash goes tight = you stop dead and stand still. Slack returns = say 'yes', treat at your knee, walk on. 10 min max, boring on purpose.
3. 'Find it' — toss a treat on the ground and say 'find it'. This becomes your emergency reactivity tool. 20 reps.

Weekends: one 30-45 min decompression sniff walk on a long line somewhere empty (early morning, quiet park edge, school grounds after hours). Border collie mix needs the mental drain — an under-exercised collie is a more reactive collie.

Also this week: 15 min of nose work or a puzzle feeder daily. Sniffing lowers arousal more than running does.

WEEK 1 SUCCESS = he turns to his name instantly, and 'find it' makes his nose hit the floor within a second.

subtasks.title: Week 2 — Find his threshold distance, start engage-disengage
subtasks.description:
GOAL: change what another dog PREDICTS, from a distance where he can still think.

Find the threshold: park where you can see dogs at a distance (edge of a dog park lot, across a wide street, a trail overlook). Watch him. Threshold = the closest distance at which he still takes a treat and can look away. That's probably 60-100 ft right now. Work there, not closer. Ever.

The drill (Engage-Disengage, 3x/week, 10-15 min only):
- Dog appears in the distance. The MOMENT he looks at it, say 'yes' and feed.
- Repeat. Soon he'll look at the dog and then snap his head back to you for the treat — that's the whole game.
- Feed him for looking, not for being quiet. You're paying him for noticing calmly.
- If he barks: you were too close. Say 'find it', walk away 20 ft, restart. No scolding — he's not being bad, he's over threshold.

End every session BEFORE he cracks. Short and successful beats long and blown up.

Leash work continues 2x10 min daily, now on the sidewalk at quiet times.

WEEK 2 SUCCESS = you know his number in feet, and he does at least a few look-then-check-back loops.

subtasks.title: Week 3 — Close the distance, add an escape route
subtasks.description:
GOAL: shave distance off the threshold and install a U-turn so you always have an exit.

1. Teach 'Let's go' U-turn (in the quiet, first): say 'let's go' in a bright voice, pivot 180 and jog 5 steps, feed. 15 reps. Then use it on walks any time a dog appears too suddenly. This is your rip cord.

2. Engage-disengage again 3x/week, but move 5-10 ft closer than last week — only if last week was going smoothly. If he barks twice in one session, back up to last week's distance and stay there another week. Going backwards is normal and not failure.

3. Parallel walking (if you have a friend with a calm dog): walk the same direction, 40+ ft apart, same pace, no greeting, no nose-to-nose. 10 minutes then stop. This is worth more than ten sidewalk encounters.

4. Loose-leash: raise the bar. Now practice on your actual walking route at a quiet hour. Add turns and stops. Reward heavily at your knee.

Do NOT let him meet other dogs head-on on leash. Tight leash + face-to-face is what created this.

WEEK 3 SUCCESS = a U-turn on cue, and threshold distance has shrunk noticeably.

subtasks.title: Week 4 — Real walks, and decide about a trainer
subtasks.description:
GOAL: put it together on a normal walk and honestly assess.

1. Two or three real neighbourhood walks with the full toolkit: front-clip harness, treats in hand, scanning ahead of him for dogs. When you spot one: mark-and-feed if he's calm, or 'let's go' U-turn if it's too close. You are his lookout — spot the dog before he does, every time.

2. Keep engage-disengage 2x this week at whatever distance is working.

3. Keep one weekend long-line sniff walk. Non-negotiable for this breed.

4. Assess honestly and write it down:
   - Can he eat treats with a dog visible at 30-40 ft?
   - Does his bark recover in seconds instead of escalating for a block?
   - Is loose-leash walking working when no dogs are around?
   If mostly yes: keep going, this works, just repeat weeks 3-4 with shrinking distance for the next two months. Realistic timeline for solid reactivity change is 3-6 months, not 4 weeks.
   If mostly no, or he's redirecting onto you/the leash: book the private trainer (see the trainer subtask) rather than grinding on alone.

WEEK 4 SUCCESS = you have a repeatable walk protocol and a clear yes/no on needing paid help.

subtasks.title: Email or call the top two trainers to book an intake consult
subtasks.description:
Do this in Week 1 if you want the class running alongside the plan, or hold until the Week 4 assessment if you'd rather try DIY first.

1) HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 — $300, 6 weeks, online evenings. Email DogTraining@hssv.org. Ask: next cohort start date and time, and — if he was adopted from HSSV — whether your complimentary adopter training covers it (have his Animal ID from the adoption paperwork ready).

2) Orion Dog Training, San Jose — free 20-minute phone consult, book via oriondogtraining.com/reactivedog. Ask: next reactive-dog or Control Unleashed class date, price (expect ~$275-295 for 6 weeks), class size, and whether 14-month adolescent collie mixes are a fit.

3) Optional if you want private in-home: D For Dogz, 650-538-3011. Ask: total cost of the Reactive Dog Foundation "Personal Coaching" option (owner-trained, not board & train), whether evening or Saturday slots exist (listed hours are Mon-Fri 9-7, Sun 9-3), and what the $420 full-program discount applies to.

Screening question for any trainer: "What do you do when he barks and lunges?" If the answer involves a prong collar, e-collar, or "correcting" him — hang up.
